concept.shortExplanation: A neuron is a weighted sum followed by one non-linear function. That is all. The weighted sum can only draw straight lines; the non-linearity is what lets stacks of them bend. ReLU passes positives through and flattens negatives, which sounds too crude to matter and turns out to be the reason deep networks train at all. Change the activation and the same weights produce a completely different shape.
concept.ahaMoment: Remove the activation function and a hundred stacked layers collapse algebraically into a single linear one. The entire depth of a deep network is only worth something because of that one bend per layer.

levels.title: Tune the Weights
levels.instructions: Set the two weights and the bias so the neuron's output matches the target curve. Every output value is the real forward computation of your current parameters.
hints: This uses the exact same activation as the target neuron, so there's a direct, findable answer rather than an approximate one — move one weight at a time and watch which one straightens out the shape of your curve to match the target's.

Get the general shape right before fine-tuning exact values: which weight controls how strongly the curve responds to the first input, which to the second, and how the bias shifts the whole thing up or down.
w0 = 1.5, w1 = −0.8, bias = 0.4 reproduces the target exactly — those are literally the weights the target curve was generated from.

levels.title: Match the Activation
levels.instructions: Each output trace was produced by one activation function. Identify which — the traces are generated live by running the same weights through each candidate.
hints: Check the output range first: sigmoid stays between 0 and 1, tanh stays between −1 and 1, and ReLU, leaky ReLU and GELU can all go arbitrarily positive. That alone eliminates two or three candidates immediately.

Among the unbounded ones: plain ReLU is exactly flat at zero for every negative input, leaky ReLU has a small but nonzero negative slope instead of flat, and GELU dips slightly below zero just before the origin before curving up — it's the only one of the three that isn't monotonic near zero.

Check in order: stays in [0,1] → sigmoid. Stays in [−1,1] → tanh. Flat at exactly zero for negatives → ReLU. Small negative slope instead of flat → leaky ReLU. Dips slightly below zero near the origin before rising → GELU.

levels.title: The Dead Neuron
levels.instructions: This ReLU neuron outputs zero for every input in the dataset and receives no gradient as a result. Diagnose it and bring it back to life without changing the activation.
hints: Nothing here is wrong about the weights' direction — the neuron's sum is just permanently negative because of how negative the bias is. Try adjusting the bias before touching the weights at all.

The probes span roughly ±2 on each input, so the weighted part of the sum only ever swings a modest amount either way — a bias of −2.9 overwhelms that completely, so every probe reads negative. Bring the bias up toward positive territory.
Raise the bias alone, leaving the weights untouched — bias = 0 already revives about 56% of probes (past two stars), and bias ≈ 1 wakes every single one of them (three stars).
